extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers of comparative religion, mythology, and anthropology
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis and synthesis of lunar myths and moon-worship across cultures, with methodological comments on how to interpret myths historically and anthropologically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of myths as historical evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditions and myths are of great importance, and indirectly throw much light on the condition of man in ancient times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use myths as 'raw material' that can illuminate ancient life and beliefs; treat them as sources that 'throw much light' rather than dismiss them as mere fable. The author argues that myths supply material out of which modern science and religion have been formed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation of revealing episodes in myth
rubrics_metrics.description: Mythic tradition tells its tales without expurgating the episodes which betray its real character to more critical observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect myths to preserve unedited or unexpurgated episodes that reveal their original character; these elements can be instructive for critical analysis and for tracing origins or cultural features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evolutionary/developmental approach to religious change
rubrics_metrics.description: The modern method in philosophy is evolution ... this process recognises no abrupt or interruptive creations, but gradual transformations from pre-existent types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret religious and mythological change as gradual transformations (variations and accretions) rather than as sudden, isolated creations. Look for continuities and 'grafts' from older beliefs into newer systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mythology tends from many gods toward one (synthesis)
rubrics_metrics.description: We must ever bear in mind that the course of mythology is from many gods toward one, that it is a synthesis, not an analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comparing traditions, use the heuristic that mythic systems often consolidate and synthesize multiple deities/traits into unified figures over time; this helps explain parallels and overlaps between pantheons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of projecting modern biases (observer projection)
rubrics_metrics.description: We in the West characterize and colour objects which we behold, as we see them through the painted windows of our predisposition or prejudice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid assuming that your cultural interpretation (e.g., seeing a 'hare' or a 'frog' on the moon) is universal. Explicitly account for observer bias and local predispositions when interpreting mythic imagery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for survivals and syncretism in 'baptized' or modern religions
rubrics_metrics.description: Baptized heathenism is often heathenism still, under another name ... No religion has fallen from heaven ... All spiritual life is primordially an inspiration or intuition from the Father of spirits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When studying contemporary or later religious practices, look for earlier pagan or mythic elements that survive or are reinterpreted; do not assume doctrinal 'purity' simply because a tradition is labeled Christian or monotheistic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish anthropomorphic imagery from literal belief
rubrics_metrics.description: Anthropomorphism, or the representation of outward objects in the form of man, ... Against this anthropomorphic materialism science lifts up its voice; for what modern philosopher ... fails to distinguish between phenomenon and fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat anthropomorphic descriptions (gods 'with forms of man') as figurative or heuristic; critically separate metaphorical representation from claims about ontological reality when reconstructing beliefs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate gendered personification critically (grammar vs culture)
rubrics_metrics.description: It may be supposed that grammatical gender has been the cause of the male and female personation of deities, when really it has been the result ... That grammar is very much younger than sexual relations is proven by the curious fact ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume grammatical gender alone explains deity-sex assignment. Examine social/sexual dynamics and cultural context as potential causes of masculine or feminine personification of celestial bodies (e.g., moon as male in many cultures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use cross-cultural distribution to assess importance
rubrics_metrics.description: Moon worship, naturally ranking below sun worship in importance, ranges through nearly the same district of culture. There are remarkable cases in which the moon is recognised as a great deity by tribes who take less account, or none at all, of the sun.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map the geographical and cultural distribution of lunar vs solar worship to understand relative importance and local emphases; note exceptions where moon worship dominates, and explore environmental or cultural reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat myths as sources for reconstructing cultural nomenclature and institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: The word for the moon ... was used to mark remote antiquity ... by the courses of the moon ancient months and years were numbered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use linguistic and ritual references in myths (names, calendar use, festivals) to infer institutional and temporal structures (e.g., lunar calendars, festival timing), corroborating with textual and archaeological evidence.
